node-production:0.prompt: An API's p99 latency spikes under load. One CPU core is pinned at 100% while the database looks idle. What's the most likely cause?
options: The database connection pool is too small
Synchronous CPU work in a request handler (e.g. huge JSON.parse, sync crypto, heavy loops) is blocking the event loop
The libuv threadpool has too many threads
The garbage collector is running on other cores
node-production:0.explanation: One saturated core plus an idle DB points at the single JS thread doing CPU work, so every other request queues behind it. A small pool would show requests waiting on DB connections, not a pinned core.

node-production:0.prompt: You started a service with `node --prof server.js` and reproduced the slowness. What do you do with the generated isolate-*.log file?
options: Open it directly in Chrome DevTools
Run `node --prof-process isolate-*.log` to get a readable summary of ticks per function
Upload it to npm audit
Pass it to `--inspect` on the next start
node-production:0.explanation: --prof writes V8 tick samples; --prof-process aggregates them into the functions where time was spent. To load a profile in DevTools, use `--cpu-prof`, which writes a .cpuprofile file.

node-production:0.prompt: In a CPU flame graph (e.g. from clinic flame or 0x), what does a wide frame at the top of a stack indicate?
options: A function that was called many times but did little work
A function spending a lot of time on-CPU itself (hot self time)
A function waiting on I/O for a long time
The oldest function in the program
node-production:0.explanation: Width is the share of samples. A frame that's wide at the top of its stack is where the CPU actually was, so it's the hot code to optimise. Flame graphs show on-CPU samples, so time spent waiting on I/O doesn't appear.

node-production:0.prompt: Which built-in API lets you continuously measure event-loop delay in production and export percentiles as metrics?
options: process.hrtime()
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()
os.loadavg()
process.memoryUsage()
node-production:0.explanation: monitorEventLoopDelay returns a histogram (min, max, mean, percentiles) of loop delay, which is ideal for dashboards and alerts. os.loadavg is system-wide CPU load and says nothing about this process's loop.

node-production:0.prompt: A login endpoint validates emails with a complex regex. Certain long, malformed inputs make the whole service unresponsive for seconds. What is this?
options: A memory leak in the regex cache
ReDoS: catastrophic backtracking in the regex blocks the event loop
DNS resolution blocking the threadpool
A slow database index
node-production:0.explanation: Patterns with nested quantifiers can backtrack exponentially on crafted input, and regex matching runs synchronously on the main thread, freezing every request. Fix it with linear-time patterns, input length limits, or a safe-regex check.

node-production:0.prompt: A report-generation endpoint does 2 seconds of pure JavaScript computation per request. What keeps other requests responsive?
options: Wrap the computation in a Promise
Mark the handler async and await the computation
Run the computation in a worker_threads pool (e.g. Piscina)
Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
node-production:0.explanation: Only a separate thread or process takes CPU work off the main event loop. A Promise executor and async functions still run on the main thread, and the libuv threadpool only runs native tasks such as fs, crypto and zlib, not your JavaScript.

The 10 ms timer can't fire while the synchronous loop holds the thread for 100 ms, so it runs about 90 ms late. Timer delays are minimums, and event-loop blocking shows up exactly like this as latency.
The Promise executor runs synchronously, so the heavy loop blocks before 'after' is logged; only the .then callback is deferred. Wrapping CPU work in a Promise doesn't offload it.

node-production:0.prompt: Which observations suggest event-loop blocking in a Node service? Select all that apply.
options: Event-loop delay p99 jumps from ~5 ms to hundreds of ms
One core is saturated while other cores are idle
Health checks time out under load even though dependencies are healthy
The database's own metrics show slow queries
node-production:0.explanation: Loop delay, a single hot core and starved health checks all point at the JS thread being busy. Slow queries in the DB's own metrics point at the database instead.

node-production:0.prompt: Which of these, run inside a request handler, block the event loop? Select all that apply.
options: JSON.stringify on a 200 MB object
fs.readFileSync of a large file
crypto.pbkdf2Sync with a high iteration count
await pool.query(sql) with the pg driver
await bcrypt.hash(pw, 12) with the native bcrypt package
node-production:0.explanation: JSON serialisation and *Sync APIs run on the main thread. A pg query is network I/O, and native bcrypt's async hash runs on the libuv threadpool, so neither blocks the loop while you await.

node-production:0.prompt: Wrapping a CPU-bound loop in an async function moves the computation off the main thread.
options: True
False
node-production:0.explanation: async only changes how results are delivered; the body runs on the same thread until its first await. CPU work needs worker_threads or a separate process.

node-production:1.prompt: What's the purpose of the 'three-snapshot' technique in Chrome DevTools when hunting a Node memory leak?
options: Measuring CPU usage at three points in time
Taking snapshots before, during and after repeated load, then looking for objects allocated between snapshots 1 and 2 that still survive in 3
Comparing three different Node versions
Forcing three full GCs to free memory
node-production:1.explanation: Objects created during the load phase that survive after load stops (and after GC) are the likely leak. A single snapshot can't tell normal caches from growth.

node-production:1.prompt: Heap usage grows steadily with traffic and never drops. The code has a module-level `const sessions = new Map()` that stores an entry per request ID. What's most likely?
options: V8's GC is broken for Maps
Entries are added but never removed, so the Map keeps every request's data reachable
Maps are always slower than objects
The leak must be in a native addon
node-production:1.explanation: Anything reachable from a module-level variable lives forever. An unbounded cache with no eviction or TTL is the most common Node leak. Add deletion, an LRU bound, or a TTL.

node-production:1.prompt: In a heap snapshot, what's the difference between an object's shallow size and its retained size?
options: Shallow size is on-disk; retained size is in-memory
Shallow size is the object's own memory; retained size is the memory that would be freed if the object were collected, including everything only it keeps alive
They're always equal for JavaScript objects
Retained size counts only strings
node-production:1.explanation: A small Map can have a tiny shallow size but a huge retained size because it's the only path to thousands of entries. Sorting by retained size finds leak roots.

node-production:1.prompt: Each request runs `bus.on('config-changed', handler)` on a long-lived EventEmitter. After a while, Node prints MaxListenersExceededWarning and memory climbs. What's going on?
options: The warning is harmless; raise setMaxListeners
A listener is added per request and never removed, so the emitter retains every handler and the closures it captures
EventEmitter leaks memory by design
The handler is too slow
node-production:1.explanation: The emitter holds strong references to its listeners, and each closure retains its request's data. Register once at startup, or remove the listener with off/once when the request ends. Raising the limit just hides the warning.

node-production:1.prompt: Container memory (RSS) keeps rising, but process.memoryUsage().heapUsed stays flat. Where should you look?
options: The JavaScript heap: take more heap snapshots
Memory outside the V8 heap, such as Buffers/ArrayBuffers (external), native addons, or allocator fragmentation
The call stack
The source code cache
node-production:1.explanation: Heap snapshots mostly show the JS heap. Growth in RSS but not heapUsed points at external or arrayBuffers memory (check those fields), native modules, or fragmentation. Flat heapUsed makes a JS-object leak unlikely.

node-production:1.prompt: Why be careful when taking a heap snapshot of a production Node instance?
options: Snapshots expose environment variables to the network
Writing a snapshot blocks the process and can need memory comparable to the heap, risking OOM, so take it from an instance out of rotation
Snapshots permanently disable the GC
It only works on Windows
node-production:1.explanation: Snapshotting is synchronous and memory-hungry, so a busy pod near its limit may freeze or get OOM-killed. Drain one instance first. Snapshots do contain heap data such as secrets in memory, so store them securely too.

node-production:1.prompt: A Node service runs in a container with a 1 GiB memory limit and gets OOM-killed by the kernel without a JavaScript heap error. Which setting helps most?
options: --max-old-space-size set to about 2048
--max-old-space-size set to roughly 70–80% of the container limit, leaving room for non-heap memory
--stack-size=65500
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1
node-production:1.explanation: RSS includes the heap plus buffers, code, stacks and native memory. Capping old space below the limit makes V8 collect harder (or fail with a visible heap error) before the kernel kills the container. Setting it above the limit makes kills more likely.

node-production:1.prompt: Which patterns commonly cause memory leaks in long-running Node services? Select all that apply.
options: A setInterval that's never cleared and captures a large object
Pushing every request's log entry into a global array
A listener on a long-lived emitter whose closure references req/res
A WeakMap keyed by request objects
Local variables in a function that has returned
node-production:1.explanation: Timers, globals and long-lived listeners keep their references reachable forever. WeakMap entries go away with their keys, and locals of a finished call are collectable unless a closure retains them.

node-production:1.prompt: Which are valid ways to capture a heap snapshot from a Node process? Select all that apply.
options: Start with --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 and send that signal
Call v8.writeHeapSnapshot() from an admin-only code path
Attach Chrome DevTools via --inspect and use the Memory tab
Start with --prof
node-production:1.explanation: The signal flag, the v8 module API and the inspector all produce .heapsnapshot files. --prof records CPU ticks, not heap contents.

node-production:1.prompt: If heapUsed rises during the first minutes after startup, that alone proves a memory leak.
options: True
False
node-production:1.explanation: Warm-up fills caches, JIT code and connection pools. A leak is growth that continues under steady load and survives GC, which you confirm by comparing snapshots over time.

node-production:1.prompt: The --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit flag can make Node write heap snapshots automatically as the process approaches its heap limit.
options: True
False
node-production:1.explanation: --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N writes up to N snapshots when the heap nears the limit, capturing evidence of an OOM you can't reproduce on demand. Writing a snapshot needs extra memory, so it may not always succeed.

node-production:2.prompt: What does Node's cluster module give you?
options: Multiple threads sharing one heap
Multiple worker processes, each with its own event loop and memory, sharing a listening port
Automatic distribution of one request across all cores
A distributed cache across machines
node-production:2.explanation: cluster forks processes, and the primary distributes incoming connections to them (round-robin by default except on Windows). Each request still runs in one worker. Shared memory between threads is worker_threads territory.

node-production:2.prompt: You deploy a Node API on Kubernetes. What's the usual recommendation for using CPU cores?
options: Use cluster inside every pod to fork one worker per host core
Run one Node process per container, set CPU requests/limits, and scale replicas (HPA)
Run all services in a single pod
Disable the event loop and use threads
node-production:2.explanation: The orchestrator already provides process supervision, restarts and load balancing, so one process per container keeps metrics, health checks and memory limits simple. Forking per host core inside a pod often oversubscribes the CPU limit.

node-production:2.prompt: An app stores sessions in process memory and runs 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Users get randomly logged out. What's the proper fix?
options: Add more instances
Move sessions to a shared store (e.g. Redis) or use stateless signed tokens
Lower the session TTL
Use cluster instead of separate instances
node-production:2.explanation: Each instance sees only its own sessions, so a request routed elsewhere looks logged out. Sticky sessions hide this but break on restarts and uneven load. Externalising state is the real fix, and cluster has the same problem.

node-production:2.prompt: A Socket.IO chat runs on 3 Node instances. Messages sent by a user on instance A don't reach users connected to instance B. What's the standard solution?
options: Increase the WebSocket timeout
Use a pub/sub adapter (e.g. the Redis adapter) so instances broadcast events to each other
Run a single instance only
Switch to HTTP/2
node-production:2.explanation: Each instance only knows its own sockets. A pub/sub backplane relays broadcasts to every instance. Sticky sessions are still needed for long-polling transports, but they don't solve cross-instance fan-out.

node-production:2.prompt: In PM2 cluster mode, how do `pm2 reload app` and `pm2 restart app` differ?
options: They're identical
reload replaces workers one by one, keeping some up for zero downtime; restart kills and restarts all of them
restart is zero-downtime; reload drops connections
reload only re-reads environment variables
node-production:2.explanation: reload rolls through workers, waiting for each new one to be ready before stopping the old one. That works best when the app handles SIGINT gracefully. restart stops everything at once, causing a brief outage.

node-production:2.prompt: Inside a container limited to 2 CPUs on a 64-core host, code forks `os.cpus().length` cluster workers. What happens?
options: It forks 2 workers, because os.cpus respects cgroup limits
It may fork 64 workers that compete for 2 CPUs, adding memory use and context switching; size from configuration or os.availableParallelism() and verify
Node refuses to start
The kernel adds more CPUs
node-production:2.explanation: os.cpus() reports the host's logical CPUs, not the container's CPU quota. Oversubscribing wastes memory and hurts latency. Set the worker count explicitly from config and check what availableParallelism reports in your environment.

node-production:2.prompt: Under load, a service that calls `crypto.pbkdf2` (async) and `fs.readFile` heavily shows rising latency even though CPU is not saturated. What's a likely bottleneck?
options: The V8 heap size
The libuv threadpool, which has 4 threads by default and is shared by fs, crypto, zlib and dns.lookup
The number of TCP sockets
The microtask queue
node-production:2.explanation: Async fs and crypto tasks queue for the threadpool. With 4 threads, slow tasks starve others. Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (set before the pool is first used) or reduce threadpool-bound work. Network sockets don't use the pool.

node-production:2.prompt: You scale a Node service from 1 instance to 5. Which features break or change behaviour unless you redesign them? Select all that apply.
options: In-memory rate-limit counters
In-memory session storage
A node-cron job scheduled inside the app process
Stateless JWT verification with a shared secret
node-production:2.explanation: Counters and sessions split across instances, and in-process cron runs 5 times. JWT verification needs only the shared secret or public key, so every instance can verify on its own.

node-production:2.prompt: Which statements comparing cluster and worker_threads are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster workers are separate processes with separate heaps
worker_threads can share memory via SharedArrayBuffer
cluster is the right tool to offload one CPU-heavy request so the same process stays responsive
Cluster workers can all listen on the same port
node-production:2.explanation: cluster scales request handling across processes on one port; worker_threads run CPU work inside a process and can share memory. A CPU-heavy request in a cluster worker still blocks that worker; offloading it needs a worker thread.

node-production:2.prompt: In Kubernetes, a common approach is to run one Node process per container and scale with replicas, rather than using the cluster module inside each pod.
options: True
False
node-production:2.explanation: Orchestrators already supervise and load-balance processes, so one process per pod keeps resource limits, health checks and metrics accurate. Cluster is more useful on a VM without an orchestrator.

node-production:2.prompt: With the cluster module, workers share in-memory JavaScript objects, so a Map cache filled in one worker is visible to the others.
options: True
False
node-production:2.explanation: Each worker is a separate process with its own heap. Shared state needs IPC messages or an external store such as Redis.

node-production:3.prompt: How should readiness and liveness probes differ for a Node API on Kubernetes?
options: They should run the same check
Readiness says 'can I take traffic now?' (fails while warming up or draining); liveness says 'is the process wedged?' and should be cheap and local
Liveness should check every downstream dependency
Readiness failures restart the pod
node-production:3.explanation: A failing readiness probe removes the pod from load balancing without killing it; a failing liveness probe restarts it. Mixing them up causes needless restarts.

node-production:3.prompt: A team's liveness probe pings the database. During a 2-minute DB outage, every API pod restarts repeatedly. What went wrong?
options: The probe timeout was too long
A shared dependency failure made every liveness check fail, so Kubernetes restarted healthy processes, adding cold starts and reconnect storms
Kubernetes doesn't support HTTP probes
The pods lacked enough memory
node-production:3.explanation: Restarting doesn't fix the database and makes recovery worse. Dependency checks belong in readiness (if anywhere); liveness should only detect a stuck process, such as an unresponsive event loop.

node-production:3.prompt: On SIGTERM a Node HTTP server calls server.close(), but the process takes much longer to exit than expected. Clients use HTTP keep-alive. Why?
options: server.close() closes all connections immediately

close() stops new connections but waits for open ones; long keep-alive connections, and active requests on them, delay the callback, so use closeIdleConnections()/closeAllConnections() with a deadline
SIGTERM is ignored by Node
keep-alive is disabled in Node
node-production:3.explanation: Since Node 19, close() also closes idle connections, but connections with in-flight requests stay open until they finish. Older versions waited on idle keep-alive sockets too. A deadline then closeAllConnections() bounds shutdown time.

node-production:3.prompt: A Dockerfile ends with `CMD node server.js` (shell form). The SIGTERM handler never runs on `docker stop`, and the container is killed after 10 seconds. Why?
options: Node can't handle SIGTERM
Shell form runs `/bin/sh -c`, which becomes PID 1 and doesn't forward SIGTERM to node; use exec form `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` or an init such as tini
docker stop sends SIGKILL first
The handler must be async
node-production:3.explanation: With shell form, the shell receives the signal and node never sees it, so Docker falls back to SIGKILL after the grace period. Exec form makes node itself receive SIGTERM.

node-production:3.prompt: Why do graceful-shutdown handlers often include `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref()`?
options: To make shutdown faster in the normal case
To force exit if draining hangs (stuck sockets, a pending query), and unref() so the timer itself doesn't keep the process alive
To restart the process after 10 seconds
To delay SIGKILL
node-production:3.explanation: Without a deadline, one hung connection blocks exit until the orchestrator sends SIGKILL. unref() means a clean drain can exit naturally before the timer fires. Keep the deadline below the platform's grace period.

node-production:3.prompt: By default, how long does Kubernetes wait after sending SIGTERM to a pod before sending SIGKILL?
options: 5 seconds
30 seconds (terminationGracePeriodSeconds)
2 minutes
It never sends SIGKILL
node-production:3.explanation: The default grace period is 30 s, covering any preStop hook plus your shutdown. Your drain deadline must fit inside it, or the process is killed mid-drain.

node-production:3.prompt: Why do many Kubernetes deployments add a short preStop sleep (e.g. 5–10 s) before the app starts shutting down?
options: To let the JIT warm up
Endpoint removal propagates to load balancers and kube-proxy asynchronously, so traffic can still arrive briefly after termination starts
To flush the npm cache
Kubernetes requires it for SIGTERM to work
node-production:3.explanation: Pod deletion and endpoint updates happen in parallel. If the app closes its listener immediately, late-routed requests get connection errors. Sleeping first lets routing converge before draining.

node-production:3.prompt: Which are good practices for health endpoints? Select all that apply.
options: Readiness checks the dependencies needed to serve requests
Liveness is cheap and local, with no deep downstream calls
Health endpoints go through the normal auth middleware so only admins can call them
Readiness returns 503 while the instance is draining
node-production:3.explanation: Probes are unauthenticated calls from the kubelet or load balancer, so put health routes before auth (and expose no sensitive data). Returning 503 during drain takes the instance out of rotation.

node-production:3.prompt: On SIGTERM, which tasks belong in a Node service's graceful shutdown? Select all that apply.
options: Let in-flight HTTP requests finish
Close the BullMQ worker so the current job completes and no new ones are picked up
Flush buffered logs and metrics
Run pending database migrations
node-production:3.explanation: Shutdown should finish in-flight work and release resources (pools, queues, telemetry). Migrations are a deploy step; running them during shutdown risks a partial migration when SIGKILL lands.

node-production:3.prompt: A Node process can register process.on('SIGKILL', ...) to run cleanup before being killed.
options: True
False
node-production:3.explanation: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) can't be caught or ignored; the kernel ends the process immediately. That's why cleanup must happen on SIGTERM within the grace period.

node-production:3.prompt: Calling process.exit() immediately after server.close(), without waiting for its callback, can drop in-flight requests.
options: True
False
node-production:3.explanation: server.close() only stops accepting new connections and returns at once. Exiting immediately kills requests still in progress. Exit in the close callback, or after a deadline.

node-production:4.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per calendar minute. What burst can a client achieve?
options: At most 100 in any 60-second span
Up to 200 in about two seconds, by sending 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00
Unlimited, because windows reset
At most 50 per 30 seconds
node-production:4.explanation: Counters reset at window boundaries, so two full windows can be spent back to back. Sliding-window or token-bucket limiters smooth this out.

node-production:4.prompt: What's the main trade-off between a sliding-window log limiter and a sliding-window counter limiter?
options: The log is approximate; the counter is exact
The log stores a timestamp per request (exact but O(requests) memory); the counter weights the previous window's count (approximate but O(1) memory)
Neither works with Redis
The counter allows unlimited bursts
node-production:4.explanation: A log in a sorted set per key gives precise limits but grows with traffic. The counter estimates using current + previous × overlap, which is cheap and usually accurate enough.

node-production:4.prompt: A Redis limiter runs `INCR key` and then, as a separate command, `EXPIRE key 60` whenever INCR returns 1. What can go wrong, and what's the fix?
options: Nothing: Redis is single-threaded, so the pair is atomic
If the process crashes between the two commands the key never expires and the client is locked out; make it atomic with a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC
INCR doesn't work on missing keys
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero
node-production:4.explanation: Each command is atomic, but the pair isn't. A crash or network failure between them leaves a counter with no TTL. A Lua script (or MULTI) runs both together. INCR creates missing keys at 0 before incrementing.

node-production:4.prompt: A hot cache key (the homepage feed) expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once. What's this called and how do you mitigate it?
options: Cache poisoning; validate cache input
Cache stampede; coalesce with a per-key lock or single-flight, refresh early, or add TTL jitter
Write-behind; switch to write-through
Hot partition; add more shards
node-production:4.explanation: Simultaneous misses on one key cause a stampede. Single-flight lets one request rebuild while others wait or serve stale data, and jitter avoids synchronised expiries.

node-production:4.prompt: With cache-aside, what's the generally safer way to handle an update?
options: Update the cache first, then the database
Update the database, then delete the cache key so the next read repopulates it
Update only the cache, and sync the DB nightly
Write the new value to the cache, then the database, in parallel
node-production:4.explanation: Deleting after the DB commit avoids caching a value whose DB write failed, and narrows race windows compared with setting the value. Writing the cache first can leave it holding a value that never reached the database.

node-production:4.prompt: What should an HTTP API return when a client exceeds its rate limit?
options: 403 Forbidden
429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header
500 Internal Server Error
503 with no headers
node-production:4.explanation: 429 tells the client it's being throttled, and Retry-After says when to try again so well-behaved clients back off. 403 implies a permissions problem and won't trigger retry logic.

node-production:4.prompt: When is an in-process LRU cache a better choice than Redis for a Node service?
options: When every instance must see the same value immediately after a write
For small, read-heavy, rarely changing data where microsecond lookups matter and brief per-instance staleness is fine
When the cached data is larger than the instance's RAM
When the cache must survive restarts
node-production:4.explanation: Local memory avoids a network hop, but each instance has its own copy, so invalidation is per instance and memory is duplicated. Shared, consistent or durable caching needs Redis.

node-production:4.prompt: This token bucket has capacity 3 and refills 1 token per second. What does it print?
node-production:4.explanation: Three tokens allow a burst of 3 at t = 0; the 4th is denied. By t = 1.5, 1.5 tokens have refilled, enough for one more request but not two. The bucket allows bursts up to capacity and then a steady rate.

node-production:4.prompt: This LRU cache with capacity 2 uses a Map's insertion order. What does it print?
node-production:4.explanation: get('a') moves 'a' to the end, so 'b' becomes least recently used and is evicted when 'c' arrives. The remaining order is a, c. A Map's insertion order gives an O(1) LRU without a linked list.

node-production:4.prompt: Which caching pitfalls should you guard against? Select all that apply.
options: The cache key must include every input that changes the response (user, locale, query params)
Add jitter to TTLs so many keys don't expire at the same moment
Cache 5xx error responses with the same long TTL as successful ones
Never store per-user data under a shared key, or users will see each other's data
node-production:4.explanation: Missing key dimensions serve wrong data, synchronised expiry causes stampedes, and shared keys for personal data are a privacy bug. Errors should be uncached or cached briefly (negative caching), not kept for the normal TTL.

node-production:4.prompt: An Express app behind a load balancer that rate-limits by req.ip may end up throttling all users as one client unless 'trust proxy' is configured correctly.
options: True
False
node-production:4.explanation: Without trust proxy, req.ip is the proxy's address, so everyone shares one bucket. Configure it for your proxy hops only; trusting X-Forwarded-For blindly lets clients spoof their IP.

node-production:5.prompt: BullMQ provides at-least-once processing. What does that require from your job processors?
options: Nothing: duplicates can't happen
They should be idempotent, because a job can run more than once (e.g. after a crash or stall)
They must finish in under 1 second
They must run in a separate container
node-production:5.explanation: If a worker dies after doing the work but before acknowledging it, the job is retried. Use idempotency keys or upserts so a second run is harmless, such as not charging a card twice.

node-production:5.prompt: BullMQ logs that a job 'stalled' and processes it again on another worker. What's a common cause?
options: The Redis key was too long
The worker's event loop was blocked by CPU work (or the worker crashed), so it couldn't renew the job lock before it expired
The job had too many attempts
The queue name had uppercase letters
node-production:5.explanation: Workers periodically renew a lock on active jobs. A blocked event loop or a dead process misses renewal, so the job is treated as stalled and moved back to wait. Use sandboxed processors or worker threads for CPU-heavy jobs.

node-production:5.prompt: You want an email job retried up to 5 times with increasing delays when the provider times out. Which BullMQ job options do that?
options: { attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 } }
{ retry: true }
{ repeat: { every: 1000 }, limit: 5 }
{ priority: 5 }
node-production:5.explanation: attempts caps total tries and exponential backoff spaces them out (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...). repeat schedules recurring new runs, which isn't retrying a failure.

node-production:5.prompt: A webhook handler may receive the same event twice and enqueues a job each time. How can you make BullMQ ignore the duplicate?
options: Give the queue a unique name per event
Use the event's ID as a custom jobId; adding a job whose jobId already exists in the queue is a no-op
Set attempts: 1
Use a delayed job
node-production:5.explanation: Custom job IDs dedupe while the original job is still stored. Once it's removed (e.g. removeOnComplete), the same ID can be added again, so the processor should still be idempotent.

node-production:5.prompt: A BullMQ Worker is created with { concurrency: 50 }. When does that help, and when not?
options: It always makes jobs 50× faster
It helps I/O-bound jobs (many awaits in flight on one event loop) but not CPU-bound jobs, which still share one thread
It starts 50 processes
It only affects delayed jobs
node-production:5.explanation: Concurrency lets one worker interleave up to 50 jobs at their await points. CPU-bound processors serialise on the event loop and can stall; use sandboxed processors or more worker processes for those.

node-production:5.prompt: Which Redis maxmemory-policy should the Redis instance backing BullMQ use?
options: allkeys-lru
volatile-ttl
noeviction
allkeys-random
node-production:5.explanation: BullMQ stores queue state in Redis keys. Evicting them under memory pressure silently loses or corrupts jobs. noeviction makes writes fail loudly instead, so give the queue its own instance rather than sharing one with an LRU cache.

node-production:5.prompt: An order service enqueues 'send-confirmation' before its database transaction commits. Sometimes the worker can't find the order. What's the robust fix?
options: Add a 2-second delay to every job
Enqueue only after commit, ideally via a transactional outbox (write an outbox row in the same transaction and have a relay enqueue it)
Retry with attempts: 100
Read the order from the cache instead
node-production:5.explanation: The worker raced the uncommitted transaction. An outbox ties 'order exists' and 'job will be sent' to one commit, which also covers crashes between commit and enqueue. Delays and retries only mask the race.

node-production:5.prompt: A nightly cleanup task runs via node-cron inside a web app scaled to 4 instances, so it runs 4 times. What's a better approach?
options: Use setInterval instead
Use a BullMQ job scheduler (repeatable job) stored in Redis, so one scheduled job is created and a single worker processes each run
Run it only on the instance with the lowest PID
Increase the cron interval by 4×
node-production:5.explanation: Scheduling state in Redis means one job per tick no matter how many instances run. Electing the 'lowest PID' doesn't work across machines. A platform scheduler (e.g. Vercel or Kubernetes CronJob) is another valid option.

node-production:5.prompt: What should go into a BullMQ job's data payload? Select all that apply.
options: The order ID rather than a full snapshot of the order
Raw third-party API keys the worker needs
Small, JSON-serialisable values
An idempotency key for the side effect
node-production:5.explanation: Payloads live in Redis and show up in dashboards, so keep them small and reference data by ID (the worker reads fresh state). Secrets belong in the worker's environment or secret manager, not in job data.

node-production:5.prompt: Which statements about BullMQ failure handling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: After all attempts are exhausted, the job moves to the failed set
removeOnComplete / removeOnFail limit how many finished jobs Redis keeps
Throwing inside the processor fails that attempt and schedules a retry if attempts remain
BullMQ guarantees exactly-once processing, so idempotency is unnecessary
node-production:5.explanation: Failed jobs remain inspectable, retention options keep Redis memory bounded, and a throw is how a processor signals failure. Delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once.

node-production:5.prompt: A BullMQ worker that runs heavy synchronous CPU work inside its processor can cause its own jobs to be marked as stalled.
options: True
False
node-production:5.explanation: Lock renewal runs on the same event loop. If the processor blocks it long enough, the lock expires and the job is considered stalled, even though the worker is still running it.

node-production:6.prompt: This naive deep merge receives attacker-controlled JSON. What does it print?
node-production:6.explanation: JSON.parse creates an own key named '__proto__'. The merge then reads t['__proto__'], which is Object.prototype, and writes isAdmin onto it, so every object now has isAdmin === true. Block __proto__, constructor and prototype keys, or validate with a schema.

node-production:6.prompt: Which is the most robust defence against prototype pollution in a JSON API?
options: Wrap merges in try/catch
Validate request bodies against a strict schema (e.g. zod) that only allows known keys, and avoid recursive merges of untrusted objects
Call Object.freeze on the request body
Lowercase all keys
node-production:6.explanation: An allowlist schema drops unexpected keys like __proto__ before they reach merge or assign code. Freezing the body doesn't protect Object.prototype, and nothing throws, so try/catch catches nothing.

node-production:6.prompt: What does adding helmet() to an Express app protect against?
options: SQL injection
It sets security-related HTTP headers (e.g. Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options)
Rate limiting of brute-force attacks
Validation of request bodies
node-production:6.explanation: helmet configures response headers that reduce XSS, clickjacking and MIME-sniffing risks. It doesn't touch your queries or inputs, so injection still needs parameterisation and validation.

node-production:6.prompt: A login route runs `User.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password })` with MongoDB. Why is this dangerous beyond storing plaintext passwords?
options: findOne is slow
An attacker can send { "password": { "$ne": null } }, an operator object that matches any password (NoSQL injection)
Mongo can't query two fields
Email isn't indexed
node-production:6.explanation: JSON bodies can contain objects, and Mongo interprets $-prefixed keys as operators. Validate that fields are strings (zod), consider sanitizeFilter, and compare password hashes in code.

node-production:6.prompt: Why should CI install dependencies with `npm ci` rather than `npm install`?
options: npm ci skips security checks to run faster
npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies and fails if it doesn't match package.json, giving reproducible builds
npm ci upgrades everything to latest
npm ci doesn't need a lockfile
node-production:6.explanation: npm install can rewrite the lockfile and resolve newer versions within your ranges, so CI might build with code you never reviewed. npm ci is strict and deterministic.

node-production:6.prompt: A 'fetch preview for URL' feature lets users submit any URL, which the server fetches. What's the main risk?
options: XSS in the user's browser
SSRF: the server can be steered to internal addresses such as cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) or admin services
CSRF on the preview endpoint
Higher bandwidth bills only
node-production:6.explanation: The server's network position is the attack surface. Mitigate with allowlists, blocking private and link-local ranges after DNS resolution, re-checking redirects, and timeouts.

node-production:6.prompt: Why compare an incoming HMAC signature with crypto.timingSafeEqual instead of ===?
options: === can't compare Buffers
=== can return early at the first differing byte, leaking through timing how much of the signature matched
timingSafeEqual is faster
timingSafeEqual also decrypts the payload
node-production:6.explanation: Early-exit comparisons let attackers guess a secret byte by byte from response times. timingSafeEqual takes time independent of where the inputs differ (it requires equal-length Buffers).

node-production:6.prompt: When verifying JWTs with the jsonwebtoken library, why pass an explicit `algorithms: ['HS256']` option (or whatever you issue)?
options: It makes verification faster
It prevents algorithm-confusion attacks where a token's header picks a different algorithm than the server intended
It's required to read the payload
It encrypts the token
node-production:6.explanation: If the verifier trusts the token's alg header, attackers can try 'none' or RS/HS confusion. Pinning the expected algorithms rejects such tokens. JWTs are signed, not encrypted.

node-production:6.prompt: Which practices reduce npm supply-chain risk? Select all that apply.
options: Commit package-lock.json and install with npm ci
Review npm audit output and automated update PRs
Use --ignore-scripts where install scripts aren't needed
Set dependency versions to 'latest' so fixes arrive automatically
node-production:6.explanation: Lockfiles pin reviewed versions, audits flag known CVEs, and skipping install scripts blocks a common malware vector. 'latest' pulls whatever is published, including a compromised release.

node-production:6.prompt: Which are sound input-handling practices for a Node API? Select all that apply.
options: Validate inputs against an allowlist schema (types, lengths, formats)
Use parameterised queries instead of string concatenation
Encode output for its context (HTML, URL, shell) when rendering
Strip the substring '<script>' from inputs and treat them as safe
node-production:6.explanation: Validation, parameterisation and context-aware encoding are the layered defence. Blacklist filters are trivially bypassed (event handlers, casing, encodings).

node-production:6.prompt: Setting a request body size limit (e.g. express.json({ limit: '100kb' })) helps mitigate denial of service from huge JSON payloads.
options: True
False
node-production:6.explanation: JSON.parse is synchronous and memory-hungry, so a multi-megabyte body can block the loop and spike memory. A limit rejects oversized bodies early with 413.

node-production:7.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'Is Node.js single-threaded?' What's the most accurate answer?
options: Yes, everything including I/O runs on exactly one thread
Your JavaScript runs on one main thread per event loop, but Node also uses the libuv threadpool, OS async I/O and V8 background threads (e.g. GC)
No, every request gets its own thread
Only when cluster is disabled
node-production:7.explanation: The single-threaded part is JS execution. Native work runs elsewhere, and worker_threads add more JS threads. Saying 'everything on one thread' misses how async fs and crypto actually work.

node-production:7.prompt: Which of these operations run on the libuv threadpool rather than through OS-level async I/O?
options: TCP socket reads for an HTTP server
fs.readFile, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib compression and dns.lookup
setTimeout callbacks
Promise resolution
node-production:7.explanation: File system calls, some crypto, zlib and getaddrinfo-based dns.lookup use the threadpool. Network sockets use epoll, kqueue or IOCP directly. Timers and promises are event-loop and V8 mechanisms.

node-production:7.prompt: A team proposes Node for a service where each request runs about 2 s of numeric simulation in JavaScript, at hundreds of requests per second. What's the strongest senior response?
options: Node is fine; async/await makes it parallel
On the main thread this serialises requests; offload to a worker-thread pool or a separate compute service, or pick a runtime built for CPU parallelism
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 128
Use more promises
node-production:7.explanation: CPU-bound work blocks the event loop, so throughput is capped at about one simulation per core. Offloading or choosing a better-suited runtime solves that; async syntax and the threadpool size don't run your JS in parallel.

node-production:7.prompt: Why can one Node process hold ~10,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with modest memory, where a naive thread-per-connection server struggles?
options: Node compresses connections
An idle connection in Node is just a socket plus a small object watched by the event loop, while each OS thread reserves its own stack and adds scheduling overhead
Node limits connections to 1,000
WebSockets don't use TCP
node-production:7.explanation: Thread-per-connection pays per-thread stack memory and context switches even when idle. Event-driven I/O costs almost nothing per idle socket: the C10k argument.

node-production:7.prompt: What happens if code keeps scheduling process.nextTick callbacks recursively (each tick schedules another)?
options: Node interleaves them fairly with I/O
The nextTick queue never drains, starving I/O and timers, so the server stops responding
Node throws after 1,000 ticks
They move to the threadpool
node-production:7.explanation: nextTick callbacks run before the loop continues to the next phase. A self-renewing tick chain therefore blocks I/O indefinitely. Use setImmediate to yield between chunks of work.

The then callback logs synchronously first. While V8 is draining the microtask queue, the newly queued promise job runs before Node gets a chance to process the nextTick queue, so 'micro' comes before 'tick'. nextTick only wins when it's queued from the main script, before the microtask drain begins.
Both timers start immediately and run concurrently. 'b' resolves after 10 ms, so it's pushed first, then 'a'. Concurrent I/O waits overlap, which is why Node handles many slow downstream calls well.

node-production:7.prompt: Which statements about Node's concurrency model are correct? Select all that apply.
options: V8 executes JavaScript on a single thread per isolate
Each worker_thread has its own V8 isolate and event loop
The libuv threadpool has 4 threads by default
Incoming HTTP socket reads go through the libuv threadpool
node-production:7.explanation: One isolate means one JS thread; worker threads get their own isolate and loop; UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE defaults to 4. Network sockets use OS readiness notifications (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), not the threadpool.

node-production:7.prompt: An interviewer asks how you'd handle a CPU-heavy endpoint in a Node API. Which are good answers? Select all that apply.
options: Run the work in a worker_threads pool (e.g. Piscina)
Push it onto a queue and process it in a separate worker service
Split the work into chunks and yield with setImmediate between them
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so the JavaScript runs on more threads
node-production:7.explanation: Threads, out-of-band workers and cooperative chunking all keep the main loop responsive. The libuv threadpool only runs native tasks, never your JavaScript functions.

node-production:7.prompt: Why is continuing to serve traffic after an 'uncaughtException' handler fires considered a bad idea?
options: Node forbids it
The process may be in an unknown state (half-updated data, leaked resources), so log, try to finish in-flight work briefly, exit, and let the supervisor restart it
It doubles memory use
It disables the event loop
node-production:7.explanation: An exception that escaped every handler means invariants may be broken. Node's docs recommend uncaughtException only for synchronous cleanup before exiting. Restarting a clean process is safer than limping on.

node-production:7.prompt: Increasing UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE speeds up a CPU-heavy pure-JavaScript loop inside a request handler.
options: True
False
node-production:7.explanation: Pure JS runs on the main thread regardless of threadpool size. The pool helps only native threadpool work like fs, crypto.pbkdf2 and zlib.
